title: THE JESUS IN THE PICTURE… OR THE JESUS YOU ACTUALLY WORSHIP?
paragraphs: THE JESUS IN THE PICTURE… OR THE JESUS YOU ACTUALLY WORSHIP?

What if the image hanging on your wall is not the greatest danger—but what your heart has quietly begun to trust? A biblical examination of Exodus 20:4–5, Colossians 1:15, and the line between remembering Christ and replacing Him.
There is a picture of Jesus hanging in someone's home tonight.

Perhaps it shows Him with a crown of thorns, blood running down His forehead. Perhaps His arms are stretched wide, welcoming the broken. Perhaps He is carrying a lamb, sitting among children, or standing at a door that seems to have no handle.
A mother looks at that picture while praying for her son who has wandered from God.
A grieving widow looks at it and remembers the Savior who promised never to forsake her.
A little child points toward it and asks, “Mommy, is that Jesus?”
And somewhere else, another Christian sees the same picture and feels deeply troubled.
“Didn't God command us not to make images?”
Suddenly, something that seemed so innocent becomes a question of obedience.
Is the picture helping someone remember Jesus?
Or is it slowly teaching the heart to worship something human hands have made?
And what happens when two Christians who genuinely love the same Savior arrive at different answers?
Before you defend the picture, condemn the picture, or dismiss the entire discussion as unimportant, there is something you need to understand.
The God who forbade idols is the same God who sent His Son into the world in real human flesh.
That truth makes this question more serious—and more beautiful—than many people realize.
Because this is not ultimately about paint, paper, wood, or pixels.
It is about whether we are approaching God as He has revealed Himself, or attempting to make Him fit an image we have created.
And there is a difference.
A difference that reaches all the way into the human heart.
In Exodus 20:4–5, God declares:

“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them…” (KJV)
The original Hebrew begins with a striking prohibition:
לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל
Lo-ta'aseh lekha fesel.
“You shall not make for yourself a carved image.”
The word פֶסֶל (pesel) refers to a carved or fashioned image, particularly in the context of idolatry.
The command continues:
לֹא־תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לָהֶם וְלֹא תָעָבְדֵם
Lo-tishtachaveh lahem velo ta'ovdem.
“You shall not bow down to them or serve them.”
Notice that the command does not merely address the existence of an object.
It addresses the making of images in the context of false worship, together with bowing before them and serving them.
Yet we must be careful.

It would be too simplistic to say that God only forbids physically bowing to a statue. The command is also concerned with the attempt to represent the divine through an image and to approach God through a representation He has not authorized.
Israel's history makes that danger painfully clear.
At Mount Sinai, while Moses was receiving God's commandments, the people became impatient.
They wanted something visible.
Something tangible.
Something they could gather around.
Something they could point to and say, “There is our God.”
So Aaron fashioned a golden calf.
And in Exodus 32:4, the people proclaimed:
“These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” (KJV)
The following day was even more revealing.
Aaron announced a feast “to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5).
The Hebrew text uses the divine name, YHWH.
Think about that.
They were not necessarily announcing that they had completely abandoned the God who delivered them.
They were attempting to worship in a way that contradicted His revelation.
They attached God's name to an image God had not commanded them to make.
And heaven did not applaud their creativity.
God judged their rebellion.
Why?
Because sincerity does not automatically make worship acceptable.
Because calling something holy does not make it holy.
Because the human heart can use religious language while moving away from obedience.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
We are often quick to recognize Israel's golden calf.
But we are much slower to recognize the things we have made indispensable to our own spiritual lives.
A picture.
A religious object.
A particular atmosphere.
A favorite preacher.
A worship experience.
A tradition we have elevated beyond Scripture.
Or even a version of Jesus who never confronts our sin, never calls us to repentance, and never asks us to deny ourselves.
Sometimes the most dangerous idol is not something hanging on the wall.
Sometimes it is the Jesus we have invented in our imagination.
A Jesus who agrees with everything we want.
A Jesus who blesses everything we refuse to surrender.
A Jesus who offers comfort without holiness, forgiveness without repentance, and eternal life without the call to follow Him.
That Jesus may be popular.
But He is not the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
And if this exposes something you have quietly struggled with, you do not need to pretend otherwise.
God is not asking you to defend an illusion.
He is calling you back to the truth.
But now another question emerges.
If God forbade images in worship, why did He later command the creation of certain images?
In Exodus 25:18–20, God instructed Israel to make two golden cherubim over the mercy seat.
In Numbers 21:8–9, God commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent, which became an instrument through which God provided deliverance to those who looked in faith according to His instruction.
These passages matter because they demonstrate that the second commandment cannot reasonably mean that every artistic representation of a living creature is inherently sinful.
God Himself authorized certain representations for particular purposes.
The issue was never simply whether an object had a shape.
The issue included its religious purpose, the authority under which it was made, and how people treated it.
And Scripture gives us a remarkable warning about what happens when an originally legitimate religious object becomes an object of devotion.
Centuries later, King Hezekiah destroyed that same bronze serpent.
Why?
Because the Israelites had begun burning incense to it.
Second Kings 18:4 tells us they called it Nehushtan.
Consider the tragedy.
Something God once used in Israel's history had become an object of idolatrous devotion.
The problem was not that God's earlier instruction had been wrong.
The problem was that human beings had turned a sign associated with God's mercy into something receiving religious honor that did not belong to it.
A reminder of God's work must never become a replacement for God Himself.
That warning should humble every Christian, regardless of denomination or tradition.
Because even good things can become spiritually dangerous when they receive the trust, reverence, or devotion that belongs to the Lord.
Then we arrive at one of the most extraordinary declarations in the New Testament.
Colossians 1:15 says of Jesus Christ:
“Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.” (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου
Hos estin eikōn tou theou tou aoratou.
“Who is the image of the invisible God.”
The word εἰκών (eikōn) means image or likeness.
But Paul is not describing Jesus as a painting, sculpture, or artistic representation.
He is declaring something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ perfectly reveals the invisible God.
And the surrounding verses make His divine supremacy unmistakable.
Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through Him and for Him.
Colossians 1:17 declares that He is before all things and that all things hold together in Him.
Therefore, when Paul calls Jesus the “firstborn of all creation,” he is not teaching that Jesus was the first creature God made.
The Greek term πρωτότοκος (prōtotokos), meaning “firstborn,” carries the significance of preeminence and rank in this context.
Christ is supreme over creation because He is its Creator.
He is not one more created object within the universe.
He is the eternal Son through whom the universe exists.
And then John 1:14 gives us the wonder at the center of Christianity:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us…” (KJV)
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
The eternal Son truly became human.
Not an illusion.
Not a religious symbol.
Not a spiritual being merely pretending to have a body.
Jesus entered human history.
He could be seen.
He could be touched.
He grew tired.
He wept.
He ate with sinners.
He embraced children.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
This is the miracle of the Incarnation.
And it is precisely here that sincere Christians have historically disagreed about religious images of Christ.
Some Christians reason that because the Son truly became visible in human flesh, depicting His humanity is not necessarily a denial of His deity.
They distinguish between worship, which belongs to God alone, and the respectful use of an image to remember or teach about the person depicted.

In Eastern Orthodox and some other historic Christian traditions, icons are understood within this theological framework. The Second Council of Nicaea in AD 787 defended the veneration of icons while distinguishing that veneration from the adoration owed to God alone.

Other Christians, especially within Reformed Protestant traditions, understand the second commandment to prohibit making images of God for religious purposes, including images intended to portray Jesus Christ.
They emphasize that Jesus is not merely a human person separated from His divine nature. He is one divine Person with two natures, fully God and fully man.
Therefore, they argue, attempting to portray Christ in religious imagery raises serious theological problems, even when the artist intends only to depict His humanity.
Still other Protestant Christians distinguish between using pictures for historical illustration or biblical education and using those pictures as objects or instruments of worship.
These differences are not imaginary.
They arise from serious disagreements about how the second commandment applies after the Incarnation.

And we must be faithful enough to acknowledge that the Bible does not contain a verse saying, in those exact words, “All paintings of Jesus are forbidden,” or “All educational pictures of Jesus are permitted.”
What Scripture does give us are commands, principles, historical examples, and a revelation of Christ that must govern our conclusions.
This means we should not pretend that every detail of this debate is settled by quoting one verse without its context.
But there are truths on which Christians should be able to stand together.
No image is Jesus Himself.
No painting can capture the fullness of His divine glory.
No statue can contain His presence.
No artistic representation deserves the worship belonging to the living God.
And no Christian should be taught that an image possesses saving power.
Jesus does not become more present because we have reproduced His imagined facial features.
He is not more willing to hear prayer because we are looking at a painting.
He is not less able to save someone who has never seen a religious picture.
And the forgiveness purchased at Calvary does not travel through canvas, carved wood, or printed paper.
It comes through Jesus Christ.
The risen Lord.
The only Mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
There is another detail worth remembering.
The Bible never gives us a physical description sufficient to reconstruct Jesus' face.
He was a Jewish man who lived in first-century Judea and Galilee.
Yet Scripture does not tell us the exact shape of His eyes, the length of His hair, or the precise features of His face.
The familiar portraits seen in different cultures are artistic interpretations, not verified likenesses.
A child may learn about the crucifixion from an illustration.
But that child should also be taught that the picture is not a photograph of Jesus and that its appearance is not established by Scripture.
That distinction matters.
Because biblical teaching must not quietly turn artistic imagination into historical certainty.
And now, perhaps, we can ask the question that reaches beyond the controversy.
When you see a picture of Jesus, what happens in your heart?
Does it direct your attention toward the truths of Scripture?
Does it help you explain a biblical event to someone who is learning?
Or have you begun to treat that object as though it carries a sacred power of its own?
Do you feel that God cannot hear you unless you are facing it?
Do you believe the image itself protects your house?
Do you fear removing it because you think Christ will abandon you?
Do you direct prayer to the object or believe that the material representation possesses divine power?
If so, there is a serious spiritual problem that must be confronted.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to receive you.
But because your trust is being directed toward something that cannot save.
Psalm 115:4–8 warns about idols made by human hands, objects that have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see, and ears but cannot hear.
The living God is not like them.
He speaks.
He sees.
He hears.
He acts.
And He saves.
Yet we must also be careful not to condemn every believer who uses religious artwork as though their intentions and beliefs were identical.
A mother who uses an illustrated children's Bible to teach her daughter about Christ is not automatically doing the same thing as someone who worships a statue.
Christians disagree over whether such illustrations are appropriate, but responsible biblical reasoning requires us to distinguish the questions rather than collapse them into one accusation.
We should not declare every image innocent.
And we should not assume that every person who possesses an image is an idolater.
Romans 14 calls believers to take matters of conscience seriously, even though it does not itself settle the interpretation of the second commandment.
First Corinthians 10:14 plainly commands Christians to flee idolatry.
And John 4:24 reminds us:
“God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (KJV)
That final word matters.
Truth.
Not merely emotion.
Not merely tradition.
Not merely whatever feels spiritual.
Truth.
If your conscience is convicted that using an image of Jesus would violate God's command, do not silence that conviction simply because other Christians are comfortable with it.
If your tradition permits religious artwork, examine its use honestly under Scripture. Do not assume that longstanding practice makes every form of devotion right.
If you teach children using illustrations, make clear that the pictures are imaginative representations and that the authoritative account of Jesus comes from the Bible.
And if you discover that you have placed spiritual confidence in an object rather than in Christ, turn away from that misplaced trust.
You do not need to defend it.
You do not need to hide it.
You can repent.
And you can come to Jesus.
That is where this discussion becomes more than a theological argument.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is reading these words while carrying a secret shame.
Perhaps you have spent years surrounding yourself with Christian objects while your Bible remained unopened.
Perhaps you have worn a cross around your neck while refusing to surrender the sin weighing down your conscience.
Perhaps you have defended your religious traditions fiercely while neglecting mercy, humility, and obedience.
Or perhaps you have condemned other Christians so harshly that you have forgotten the patience and gentleness you yourself have received from God.
You may have been right about a doctrinal concern.
But have you loved your neighbor while defending it?
Have you spoken the truth without pride?
Have you allowed Scripture to examine your own heart with the same seriousness you apply to someone else's?
The danger of idolatry is not limited to people who own religious pictures.
It reaches every heart tempted to give created things the place that belongs to the Creator.
And the answer is not merely to rearrange the objects in our homes.
The answer is to return to Christ.
To know Him through His Word.
To worship the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.
To repent of sin.
To receive the grace we cannot earn.
To follow the Savior who loved us enough to give Himself for us.
Because the greatest revelation of God's love is not a painting of the cross.
It is what Jesus actually accomplished upon the cross.
He bore our sins.
He suffered for the unrighteous.
He died and rose again.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” (KJV)
That is the Gospel.
Not a religious object bringing us to God.
Not our ability to visualize His face bringing us to God.
Not our perfect understanding of every historical Christian disagreement bringing us to God.
Christ Himself brings sinners to God through His saving work.
And perhaps the most breathtaking part is this:
The Jesus whose earthly face we cannot reconstruct is not unknown to us.
We know His character through Scripture.
We know His mercy through the Gospel.
We know His holiness through His teaching.
We know His compassion through His actions.
We know His victory through His resurrection.
And by faith, we love Him even though we do not presently see Him.
First Peter 1:8 describes believers as those who love Christ without having seen Him.
Read that again.
They love Him without seeing Him.
That means the Christian life does not depend on possessing a visible likeness of Jesus.
Our faith rests upon the living Christ revealed in God's Word.
And one day, the longing of every believer will be fulfilled.
First John 3:2 declares:
“…when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.” (KJV)
We shall see Him as He is.
Not as an artist imagined Him.
Not as a culture portrayed Him.
Not as a movie depicted Him.
As He is.
The risen and glorified Lord.
The One who was crucified.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls His people to Himself.
And on that day, no painting will be necessary to persuade us of His glory.
We will behold the Savior Himself.
Until then, let us refuse both idolatry and spiritual arrogance.
Let us search the Scriptures carefully.
Let us honor Christ above every image, tradition, preference, and argument.
Let us remember that genuine worship is not measured by how many religious objects fill our homes, but by whether our hearts belong to the Lord and our lives are being transformed by His grace.
And let us never forget the scandal at the center of the Gospel.
The holy Son of God was rejected by sinners.
The innocent One was condemned.
The Author of life was crucified.
Yet what looked like the triumph of darkness became the place where God's saving purpose was accomplished.
The cross was not the end.
The tomb could not hold Him.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, people enslaved by sin can be forgiven, restored, and made new.
That is why we proclaim:
Maybe this article has challenged something you have believed for years.
Maybe it has helped you understand why Christians disagree.
Maybe it has exposed a misplaced trust.
Or maybe it has reminded you that you have spent more time arguing about representations of Jesus than actually following Jesus.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave with merely another opinion.
Leave with a deeper desire to know Christ.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray for wisdom.
Examine your worship.
And ask the Lord to reveal anything that has taken His rightful place in your heart.
There is no shame in asking fellow believers to pray.
Someone reading your words may be fighting a similar battle.
Someone may need to know that questions, repentance, and spiritual growth do not have to happen in isolation.
Because this ministry is not about winning arguments for the sake of attention.
It is about helping people encounter biblical truth and grow as disciples of Jesus.
And if these messages have helped strengthen your faith, there is another meaningful way you can participate in this work.
Think of the person reading alone at midnight.
The believer who has grown cold.
The parent praying for a wandering child.
The young Christian trying to distinguish biblical truth from religious confusion.
The person who has been wounded by others and is afraid to seek God again.
We cannot know every life a message may touch.
But we can faithfully keep sharing the truth of Christ.
We also encourage believers to remain faithful in supporting their local church and its ministries.
These products are simply tools and reminders. They do not make anyone more spiritual, and purchasing them is never a measure of faith.
The greater purpose is to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment accessible to as many people as possible.
Help us keep the conversation rooted in Scripture and centered on Christ.
Because the most important thing we could ever offer the world is not another religious product, another picture, or another argument.
It is the message of Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who forgives.
The Redeemer who restores.
The King who transforms lives.
So tonight, before you close this article, consider one final question.
If every picture of Jesus disappeared from your home tomorrow, would your relationship with Him remain?
Would you still seek Him in Scripture?
Would you still trust His promises?
Would you still confess your sins?
Would you still follow Him when obedience becomes costly?
Would you still love Him without seeing His face?
Because that is the faith we are called to cultivate.
Not faith in what our hands can produce.
But faith in the One whose hands were pierced for our salvation.
And when the day finally comes that faith gives way to sight, may we be found not clinging to an image, but belonging to the Savior it could never fully portray.
You do not need to know the shape of His face to be forever changed by the scars of His love.
